text.p: The following are the main stories from Tuesday morning's Austrian newspapers:
- European Commission demands complete abolition of Austria's controversial anonymous savings accounts.
- Doctors are planning to take the state to court at the European Court of Justice due to health ministry plans of putting specialist doctors on call over weekends and public holidays.
- There were 11,000 non-EU foreign workers fewer in Austria in July compared to the previous year. However, the number of workers from EU countries has risen during the same period.
- Economics ministry hopes a new ecological tax on cars could help car part makers receive new orders.
- Pre-tax profits of paper maker Frantschach are expected to fall below 200 million schillings this year from 874 million last year.
- Die Erste savings bank reported an operating profit of 1.371 billion schillings in the first nine months of 1996, up 14.2 percent on the year-ago period.
- A coalition for the Vienna city government should be ready any moment now -- otherwise it could mean the breakdown of talks.
- Austria will join an international force for humanitarian aid to Zaire. Talks continue over whether Austria should join NATO.
- Finance ministry received several bids for the government's 70-percent voting stake in Creditanstalt, but declined to reveal any names.
- A U.S. specialist doctor has been called in to determine the cause of President Thomas Klestil's lung problems. Doctors say the president's condition has improved.
- Due to the United States' strong economy, Austria's exports to the U.S. have jumped 13.5 percent in the first half of the year, U.S. statistics show.
- Austrians ordered some 36.5 million shares of Deutsche Telekom, while only 500,000 were allocated.
- Austria lost 10 million schillings' worth of hi-tech equipment when the Russian satellite bound for Mars crashed back to earth yesterday.
